summary_html: Agency fails to **disclose required data or reports**, obstructing transparency. Federal statutes require public reporting under CAPTA, FOIA, and Sunshine provisions. In Alabama the age of majority is 19 (Ala. Code § 26-1-1), and for child abuse and neglect reporting a "child" is a person under 18, or a person under 19 who is in need of protective services and does not qualify for adult protective services (Ala. Code § 26-14-1(3)).

key_cases.holding: The Court held that although the Alabama Open Records Act carries a presumption in favor of disclosure, FERPA preempts it as to education records, so even redacted student financial-aid forms could not be released.
key_cases.relevance: It is the governing Alabama Supreme Court statement on when the Open Records Act must yield to federal law.
key_cases.quote: Because FERPA prohibits the very release of the redacted financial-aid forms and because FERPA takes precedence over the Open Records Act, the director is entitled to a summary judgment.

key_cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
key_cases.holding: The court denied mandamus and upheld a protective order that, after in camera review, limited a parent's discovery of DHR child-abuse records in a dependency case to the names and information of expected witnesses, finding no abuse of discretion.
key_cases.relevance: The decision shows how narrowly Ala. Code 26-14-8 confidentiality is pierced even by a party in litigation.
key_cases.quote: while this court has the authority to require a judge to exercise proper discretion, we cannot dictate the exercise of that discretion absent a showing of abuse

key_cases.case_name: R.C. ex rel. Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program v. Walley
key_cases.court: United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama
key_cases.holding: The court granted the Commissioner's second motion to terminate the 1991 R.C. consent decree, finding that DHR had met both prongs of the termination clause by achieving and being able to sustain systemwide substantial compliance so that continued judicial oversight was no longer necessary.
key_cases.relevance: The opinion catalogues the reporting and data obligations DHR carried under the decree and its implementation plan.
key_cases.quote: DHR successfully has reformed its child welfare system by developing a system of care which substantially complies with the requirements of the Consent Decree and the Implementation Plan

key_cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed dependency judgments but held that Ala. Code 26-14-8(b)(8), which permits otherwise confidential child-abuse reports to be used by an attorney representing a child or a parent, applies equally in dependency cases as a matter of due process when the information is relevant at the adjudicatory phase, and that refusing to disclose informant names here was error but harmless because no relevancy was shown.
key_cases.relevance: It supplies the affirmative half of Ala. Code 26-14-8 - the statute is a confidentiality rule with a built-in litigation exception, not an absolute bar.
key_cases.quote: We consider it equally applicable to child dependency cases because it represents nothing more than due process when it is relevant information in the adjudicatory phase of the proceedings.
